column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which arrow diagram shows how genetic information flows when a cell makes a protein?
column28: The central dogma says DNA is copied into RNA, and RNA is read to build a protein. Putting protein before RNA, or skipping RNA, is the usual mix-up.
column29: The master instructions come first and the finished product comes last.

column9: Copying the code of one gene from DNA into a strand of mRNA is called ___.
column28: Transcription makes an mRNA copy of a gene. Translation is the later step where mRNA is read to build a protein, and students often swap the two words.
column29: Think of a transcript: a written copy in the same "language" of bases.

column9: Reading the codons on an mRNA and linking amino acids into a chain is called ___.
column28: Translation changes the base "language" of mRNA into the amino acid "language" of proteins. Transcription is the earlier step that makes the mRNA.
column29: This step changes one language (bases) into another (amino acids).

column9: Which nitrogen base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
column28: RNA uses uracil in the places where DNA would use thymine. Adenine and guanine are in both, and thymine is the DNA-only base.
column29: One base gets swapped out when DNA's code is copied into RNA.

column9: What is the name of the sugar in each RNA nucleotide?
column28: RNA stands for ribonucleic acid because its sugar is ribose. Deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid).
column29: The sugar's name is hidden in what the letters RNA stand for.

column9: A codon is a group of how many mRNA bases?
column28: The ribosome reads mRNA three bases at a time, and each group of three is one codon. Splitting mRNA into groups of two or four is a common mistake.
column29: Four bases have to make enough different "words" for 20 amino acids. Two-letter words only give 16.

column9: Which statement best describes a gene?
column14: A sugar found only in RNA
column15: A chain of amino acids folded into a shape
column16: A section of DNA that holds the code for building a specific protein
column17: A molecule that carries amino acids to the ribosome
column28: A gene is a stretch of DNA with the instructions for one protein. A folded chain of amino acids is the protein itself, and carrying amino acids is the job of tRNA.
column29: Genes are part of the master instructions kept in the nucleus.

column9: Match each type of RNA to its job in protein synthesis.
column14: mRNA (messenger RNA) :: Carries a copy of a gene's code from the nucleus to a ribosome
column15: tRNA (transfer RNA) :: Brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome
column16: rRNA (ribosomal RNA) :: Makes up the body of the ribosome
column28: mRNA is the message, tRNA transfers amino acids, and rRNA is part of the ribosome. Mixing up mRNA and tRNA is the most common error.
column29: Use the first letter: m for message, t for transfer, r for ribosome.

column9: Proteins are built from long chains of which smaller building blocks?
column28: Proteins are chains of amino acids. Nucleotides build DNA and RNA, fatty acids build lipids, and simple sugars build carbohydrates.
column29: Think back to the four macromolecules from biochemistry.

column9: One codon on an mRNA codes for how many amino acids?
column28: Each codon stands for exactly one amino acid (or a stop signal). Students sometimes answer three because a codon has three bases, but three bases make one amino acid.
column29: A codon has three bases, but that is not what this question asks.

column9: Which codon tells the ribosome where to begin translating an mRNA?
column28: AUG is the start codon, and it also codes for methionine. UAA and UGA are stop codons, so they end translation instead of starting it.
column29: The start codon is the only one that both starts the chain and codes for methionine.

column9: Select every codon that is a stop codon. Select all that apply.
column28: The three stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA. AUG is the start codon, UGG codes for tryptophan and UAC codes for tyrosine, even though they look similar.
column29: There are exactly three stop codons, and all of them begin with U.

column9: How many strands does a molecule of mRNA usually have?
column28: mRNA is a single strand. DNA is the double-stranded molecule, which is why students often say two.
column29: DNA is a double helix. Is mRNA the same?

column9: During transcription, a cytosine (C) on the DNA template pairs with which base in the new mRNA?
column28: C always pairs with G, in DNA and in RNA. Uracil only pairs with adenine, and thymine never goes into mRNA.
column29: C and G are partners no matter which nucleic acid you are in.

column9: During transcription, a thymine (T) on the DNA template pairs with which base in the new mRNA?
column28: T pairs with A, so a DNA T becomes an A in mRNA. The common mistake is answering U: uracil only goes across from an adenine on the DNA.
column29: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, but T on the DNA still needs its usual partner.

column9: Match each protein synthesis term to its meaning.
column14: Nuclear pore :: An opening in the nuclear envelope that mRNA passes through
column15: Peptide bond :: The link that joins one amino acid to the next
column16: Polypeptide :: A long chain of amino acids
column17: Start codon :: The codon where the ribosome begins reading
column28: mRNA exits through nuclear pores, peptide bonds join amino acids, a polypeptide is the chain they form, and the start codon marks where reading begins. Mixing up peptide bond (one link) and polypeptide (the whole chain) is common.
column29: "Poly" means many. Match that one first.

column9: Transcribe the DNA template triplet AGC into mRNA. DNA AGC → mRNA ___
column28: A→U, G→C, C→G gives UCG. Writing TCG is the common mistake: an A on the DNA pairs with U in mRNA, because RNA has no thymine.
column29: Pair each base, and remember mRNA uses U where you might expect T.

column9: A gene's template strand contains the triplet TTG. RNA polymerase places these three bases in the mRNA across from it: ___
column28: T→A, T→A, G→C gives AAC. Writing UUC is the common mistake: U pairs with an A on the DNA, not a T.
column29: A DNA T still pairs with A. U only shows up across from a DNA A.

column9: An mRNA codon reads GCA. The tRNA anticodon that pairs with it is ___.
column28: G→C, C→G, A→U gives CGU. Writing CGT is the common mistake: tRNA is RNA, so it uses U, not T.
column29: tRNA is a type of RNA. Which base does RNA use across from A?

column9: Part of a codon chart shows: GAU = Asp, GCU = Ala, GGU = Gly, GUU = Val. A ribosome reads the codon GGU. Which amino acid gets added?
column28: GGU matches Gly on the chart. All four codons start with G and end with U, so the middle base is the one that decides; reading the wrong middle letter is the usual slip.
column29: All four codons look alike. Compare the second letter carefully.

column9: Before translation can begin, a ribosome must attach to which molecule?
column17: A lipid in the cell membrane
column28: The ribosome reads mRNA, so it attaches to the mRNA. DNA stays in the nucleus and is never read directly by ribosomes, which is a common misconception.
column29: The ribosome reads codons. Which molecule has codons?

column9: In a eukaryotic cell, which molecule acts as the protected master copy of the instructions and stays inside the nucleus?
column28: DNA stays in the nucleus. The cell sends out mRNA copies instead. Students sometimes pick mRNA, but mRNA is the copy that leaves.
column29: Which molecule is copied, rather than being the copy?

column9: True or false: RNA molecules contain the base thymine (T).
column28: False. RNA uses uracil (U) in place of thymine. Thymine is found only in DNA.
column29: Think about which base takes thymine's place when DNA is copied into RNA.

column9: What is the main job of a ribosome?
column14: To store the cell's genetic information
column15: To copy a gene from DNA into mRNA
column16: To unzip the entire DNA double helix
column17: To link amino acids together in the order the mRNA codes for
column28: Ribosomes are where translation happens: they read codons and join amino acids. Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription, done by RNA polymerase in the nucleus.
column29: Ribosomes are the protein-building machines of the cell.

column9: A construction company keeps its original blueprints locked in the main office and sends photocopies of one page to the job site. In protein synthesis, the photocopies represent which molecule?
column28: The originals are the DNA, kept safe in the nucleus (the office). The photocopy that travels is mRNA. The job site would be the ribosome, and the building materials would be amino acids.
column29: Which molecule is a copy that travels away from the nucleus?

column9: Which enzyme builds the mRNA strand during transcription?
column28: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template and builds mRNA. DNA polymerase builds new DNA during replication, which is the mix-up students make most.
column29: The enzyme is named after the molecule it builds.

column9: About how many different kinds of amino acids do cells use to build their proteins?
column28: Cells use 20 different amino acids. 4 is the number of RNA bases, 64 is the number of codons and 3 is the number of bases in one codon.
column29: It is far more than the number of bases, but fewer than the number of codons.

column9: Which of these cells would need to do the most translation?
column14: A dead skin cell at the surface of your skin
column15: A gland cell that releases large amounts of a digestive enzyme
column16: A cell that mostly stores fat droplets
column17: A mature human red blood cell, which has no nucleus or ribosomes
column28: Digestive enzymes are proteins, so a cell that makes lots of them must translate a lot of mRNA. A dead cell and a red blood cell without ribosomes cannot translate at all.
column29: Enzymes are proteins. Which cell is making the most protein?

column9: Meat, eggs and beans in your diet are broken down into amino acids. What do your cells mostly do with those amino acids?
column14: Use them as the bases in mRNA
column15: Turn them into DNA for new genes
column16: Store them inside the nucleus as genes
column17: Use them at ribosomes to build the proteins your cells need
column28: Your cells reuse amino acids from food to build their own proteins during translation. Amino acids are not parts of DNA or RNA; those are made of nucleotides.
column29: Amino acids are the building blocks of one kind of macromolecule.

column9: A ribosome has finished a chain of amino acids. What must happen before the chain can work as a protein?
column14: It must return to the nucleus to be read again
column15: It must fold into a specific three-dimensional shape
column16: It must be copied back into DNA
column17: It must be broken into single nucleotides
column28: A protein's job depends on its shape, so the chain folds into a specific 3-D form. Proteins are never copied back into DNA.
column29: Think about why an enzyme's shape matters.

column9: Which of these is a protein made by protein synthesis?
column15: Insulin, the hormone that lowers blood sugar
column28: Insulin is a protein, so a gene for it is transcribed and translated. Glucose and starch are carbohydrates and cholesterol is a lipid, so they are not built by ribosomes from codons.
column29: Only one choice is a chain of amino acids.

column9: The set of three bases on a tRNA that pairs with a codon on the mRNA is called the ___.
column28: The anticodon is on tRNA and pairs with the matching codon on mRNA. Calling it the codon is the common mix-up: codons are on mRNA.
column29: It is the "opposite" of a codon.

column9: In an onion root cell, which pairing of process and location is correct?
column14: Both transcription and translation in the vacuole
column15: Transcription at ribosomes; translation in the nucleus
column16: Transcription in the nucleus; translation at ribosomes in the cytoplasm
column17: Both transcription and translation in the cell wall
column28: Onion cells are eukaryotic, so the DNA is in the nucleus where transcription happens. The mRNA then goes to ribosomes in the cytoplasm for translation. Reversing the two locations is the most common error.
column29: Where is the DNA kept? That is where it gets copied.

column9: Which statement correctly describes how DNA and RNA are alike?
column17: Both are made of nucleotides that have a phosphate, a sugar and a base
column28: DNA and RNA are both nucleic acids built from nucleotides. Uracil is only in RNA, deoxyribose is only in DNA and only DNA is usually double-stranded.
column29: Three of these choices are actually differences between DNA and RNA.

column9: Select every nitrogen base that can be found in an mRNA molecule. Select all that apply.
column28: mRNA uses A, U, G and C. Thymine is the DNA-only base, and glucose is a sugar, not a base.
column29: RNA has four bases. One DNA base is swapped out.

column9: How many mRNA bases are in 4 codons?
column28: Each codon has 3 bases, so 4 × 3 = 12 bases. Answering 4 counts codons instead of bases.
column29: Multiply the number of codons by the number of bases in one codon.

column9: A section of mRNA is 15 bases long. Every codon in it codes for an amino acid (there is no stop codon in this section). How many amino acids does it code for?
column28: 15 bases ÷ 3 bases per codon = 5 codons, and each codon codes for one amino acid. Answering 15 treats every base as an amino acid.
column29: Group the bases into threes.

column9: Put these steps of protein synthesis in order, from first to last.
column14: The finished amino acid chain folds into a protein
column15: The mRNA leaves the nucleus and travels to a ribosome
column16: RNA polymerase copies a gene into mRNA in the nucleus
column17: The ribosome reads the codons and tRNAs bring amino acids
column28: The gene is transcribed first, then the mRNA moves to a ribosome, then it is translated, and the chain folds last. Putting the ribosome before the mRNA exists is the common mistake.
column29: Nothing can be read at a ribosome until it has been copied and moved there.

column9: What happens when a ribosome reaches a stop codon on the mRNA?
column14: A tRNA brings one last amino acid called "stop"
column15: The ribosome lets go of the finished amino acid chain
column16: The ribosome goes back to the start and repeats the same codons
column17: The mRNA is changed back into DNA
column28: A stop codon does not code for any amino acid. It signals the ribosome to release the chain. Thinking the stop codon adds an amino acid is a very common error.
column29: Stop codons are not matched by any amino acid.

column9: After a ribosome adds an amino acid to the growing chain, what does it do next?
column14: Jumps back to the start codon
column15: Returns to the nucleus to read the DNA
column16: Breaks down the mRNA it just read
column17: Moves along the mRNA to the next codon
column28: The ribosome moves one codon at a time down the mRNA, adding one amino acid per codon. It never goes into the nucleus or reads DNA.
column29: Picture a reader moving through a sentence one word at a time.

column9: Which base-pairing rules are used when a tRNA anticodon pairs with an mRNA codon?
column14: A with U, and C with G
column15: A with G, and C with U
column16: A with C, and G with U
column17: A with T, and C with G
column28: Codons and anticodons are both RNA, so A pairs with U and C pairs with G. Using A with T is the common mistake, since there is no thymine in RNA.
column29: Both molecules here are RNA.

column9: A ribosome has just finished translating an mRNA. What has it made?
column15: A chain of amino acids (a polypeptide)
column16: A copy of the DNA gene
column28: Translation produces a polypeptide, a chain of amino acids. Making mRNA or copying DNA are different processes, and nucleotide chains are nucleic acids, not proteins.
column29: Translation turns the base language into a different kind of chain.

column9: The "m" in mRNA stands for ___.
column28: mRNA is messenger RNA because it carries the gene's message to the ribosome. tRNA is transfer RNA and rRNA is ribosomal RNA.
column29: This RNA delivers a message from the nucleus.

column9: Bacteria such as E. coli have no nucleus. Where does transcription happen in a bacterial cell?
column28: Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus, so their DNA sits in the cytoplasm and is transcribed there. Answering nucleus forgets that prokaryotes don't have one, and bacteria have no mitochondria.
column29: Transcription happens wherever the DNA is.

column9: During transcription, which molecule serves as the template (pattern) for the new mRNA?
column28: RNA polymerase reads one strand of the gene's DNA and builds a matching mRNA. tRNA and ribosomes are used later, in translation.
column29: The mRNA's bases are paired with the bases of the master copy.

column9: Transcribe the DNA template strand CATGGA into mRNA (type the six bases with no spaces). DNA CATGGA → mRNA ___
column20: GUACCU|GUA CCU|G U A C C U|GUA-CCU|G-U-A-C-C-U
column28: C→G, A→U, T→A, G→C, G→C, A→U gives GUACCU. Putting a T anywhere in the answer is the common mistake: mRNA has no thymine.
column29: Go one base at a time, and check that your answer has no T in it.

column9: A section of a gene's template strand reads GGCATT. Write the mRNA that RNA polymerase builds from it (six bases, no spaces): ___
column20: CCGUAA|CCG UAA|C C G U A A|CCG-UAA|C-C-G-U-A-A
column28: G→C, G→C, C→G, A→U, T→A, T→A gives CCGUAA. A common mistake is writing UU at the end: DNA T pairs with A, not U.
column29: Only a DNA A becomes a U in mRNA.

column9: Which statement correctly compares a codon and an anticodon?
column14: A codon is on tRNA, and an anticodon is on the ribosome
column15: A codon is on DNA, and an anticodon is on mRNA
column16: Both are found on mRNA, and their bases are identical
column17: A codon is on mRNA, an anticodon is on tRNA, and their bases are complementary
column28: Codons are the three-base words on mRNA. Anticodons are on tRNA and pair with them (A–U, C–G), which is how the right amino acid gets delivered. Putting codons on DNA is a frequent error.
column29: The anticodon has to pair with the codon, so they are on different molecules.

column9: Translate the mRNA AUG GCU UGU UAG. Codons: AUG = Met, GCU = Ala, UGU = Cys, UAG = stop.
column28: Read left to right from AUG: Met, Ala, Cys, then UAG stops the chain without adding an amino acid. Listing "stop" as part of the chain or dropping the first Met are the common errors.
column29: Start with AUG and read one codon at a time. Does a stop codon add anything?

column9: A DNA template triplet reads GTA. Codons: CAU = His, GUA = Val, UAC = Tyr, AUG = Met. Which amino acid will be added for this triplet?
column28: First transcribe: G→C, T→A, A→U gives the codon CAU, which is His. Choosing Val comes from looking up the DNA letters (with U for T) instead of the mRNA codon.
column29: A codon chart is read with mRNA codons, not DNA triplets. Transcribe first.

column9: How many codons are in a strand of mRNA that is 36 bases long?
column28: Each codon is 3 bases, so 36 ÷ 3 = 12 codons. Multiplying by 3 instead of dividing gives 108, which is a common slip.
column29: Split the bases into groups of three.

column9: A protein chain has 50 amino acids. Not counting the stop codon, how many mRNA bases are needed to code for it?
column28: Each amino acid needs one codon of 3 bases, so 50 × 3 = 150 bases. Answering 50 forgets that each amino acid takes three bases.
column29: One amino acid needs one codon. How many bases is that?

column9: A poison from the death cap mushroom stops RNA polymerase from working. Which process is blocked first?
column14: Transcription, because no new mRNA can be made
column15: Translation only, because ribosomes stop reading
column16: Digestion, because amino acids can't be absorbed
column17: Protein folding, because chains can't change shape
column28: RNA polymerase builds mRNA, so the first thing that stops is transcription. Translation eventually stops too, but only because no new mRNA is arriving, so choosing translation misses the first step.
column29: What is RNA polymerase's job?

column9: The antibiotic streptomycin attaches to bacterial ribosomes and stops them from working. Why does this kill the bacteria?
column14: The bacteria can no longer transcribe genes into mRNA
column15: The bacteria can no longer copy their DNA
column16: The bacteria lose their cell wall right away
column17: The bacteria can no longer translate mRNA into the proteins they need
column28: Ribosomes do translation, so blocking them stops all new proteins. Transcription would still happen, which is why the transcription choice is a trap.
column29: Which step of protein synthesis needs ribosomes?

column9: A tRNA with the anticodon CCA arrives at the ribosome. Which mRNA codon is it pairing with?
column28: C→G, C→G, A→U gives GGU. GGT is the trap: mRNA is RNA, so it has U, never T.
column29: Pair each anticodon base with its partner, using RNA bases only.

column9: Select every statement that is true about transcription. Select all that apply.
column14: It happens in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells
column15: It takes place on the ribosome
column16: It uses the enzyme RNA polymerase
column17: It links amino acids together with peptide bonds
column18: It makes an RNA copy of one gene
column19: It copies every chromosome at once
column28: Transcription uses RNA polymerase in the nucleus to copy one gene into RNA. Ribosomes and peptide bonds belong to translation, and copying every chromosome is replication, not transcription.
column29: Transcription makes RNA. Anything about amino acids belongs to a different step.

column9: Select every molecule or structure that takes a direct part in translation. Select all that apply.
column28: Translation needs the mRNA message, a ribosome to read it, tRNAs to bring amino acids and the amino acids themselves. Helicase and DNA polymerase are DNA replication enzymes.
column29: Which items are needed to read codons and build a chain?

column9: A cell in your pancreas suddenly needs a lot of one protein, fast. Which strategy makes the most sense?
column14: Turn other proteins back into mRNA
column15: Transcribe many mRNA copies of the gene, and have many ribosomes translate them
column16: Send the DNA gene out to the cytoplasm to be read directly
column17: Make extra copies of the whole set of chromosomes
column28: Many mRNA copies, each read by many ribosomes, make lots of protein quickly. DNA itself stays in the nucleus, and proteins are never turned back into mRNA.
column29: One gene can be copied into mRNA many times.

column9: A student transcribes the DNA template triplet ACG and writes TGC as the mRNA. Which statement about the answer is correct?
column14: It is wrong; the mRNA should be the same as the DNA, ACG
column15: It is wrong because mRNA uses U instead of T; the correct codon is UGC
column17: It is wrong; the correct codon is UGU
column28: A→U, C→G, G→C gives UGC. The student paired A with T, which is the DNA rule; in mRNA an A on the DNA pairs with U.
column29: Check the first base. What does a DNA A pair with in RNA?

column9: A muscle cell and a skin cell from the same person have the same DNA, yet they make different proteins. What is the best explanation?
column16: They transcribe and translate different genes
column17: One of them has no ribosomes
column28: Every body cell has the same genes, but each cell type uses (expresses) a different set of them. The bases and the genetic code are the same in both cells.
column29: Same cookbook, different recipes. Which part changes?

column9: When you look up an amino acid on a codon chart, which sequence should you look up?
column15: The amino acid's first three letters
column28: Codon charts are written in mRNA codons. Looking up the DNA triplet or the tRNA anticodon is one of the most common errors on protein synthesis problems.
column29: The chart's name tells you which molecule it uses.

column9: There are 4 different RNA bases, and a codon is 3 bases long. How many different codons are possible?
column28: Each of the 3 positions can be any of 4 bases: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. Answering 12 (4 × 3) is the common mistake.
column29: There are 4 choices for the first base, 4 for the second and 4 for the third.

column9: The codons GGU and GGC both code for the amino acid glycine. What does this show about the genetic code?
column14: One of the two codons must be a mistake
column16: More than one codon can code for the same amino acid
column17: One codon can code for several different amino acids
column28: There are more codons than amino acids, so many amino acids have several codons. It does not work the other way: each codon codes for only one amino acid.
column29: Is it one codon with two meanings, or two codons with one meaning?

column9: A scientist tags newly made mRNA with a glowing dye and watches a cell under a microscope. In what order will the glow show up?
column14: Ribosomes in the cytoplasm, then the nuclear pores, then the nucleus
column15: Mitochondria, then the nucleus, then the cell membrane
column16: Nucleus, then the nuclear pores, then ribosomes in the cytoplasm
column17: Cell membrane, then the cytoplasm, then the nucleus
column28: mRNA is made in the nucleus, leaves through nuclear pores and is read at ribosomes in the cytoplasm. Reversing the path is the common error.
column29: Start where the mRNA is made.

column9: The mRNA codon CAG codes for glutamine (Gln). Which tRNA anticodon delivers glutamine to this codon?
column28: C→G, A→U, G→C gives the anticodon GUC. GTC uses T, which RNA does not have, and CAG is just the codon copied.
column29: Pair each codon base with its RNA partner.

column9: Scientists put the human insulin gene into bacteria, and the bacteria start making human insulin that diabetics can use. Why does this work?
column15: The insulin gene is made of protein, so bacteria just copy it
column16: Bacteria already had their own insulin gene
column17: Bacteria read codons with the same genetic code as humans, so they build the same amino acid chain
column28: Almost all living things use the same codons for the same amino acids, so a bacterium translates the human gene into the human protein. The gene is DNA, not protein.
column29: If the codon AUG means Met in you, what does it mean in a bacterium?

column9: A ribosome reads the mRNA AUGCCAGGU. How is this sequence split into codons?
column28: Starting at the first base of AUG, the ribosome reads groups of three: AUG, CCA, GGU. Shifting the start by one base gives completely different codons.
column29: Begin at the start codon and count off threes.

column9: Which of these is NOT needed for transcribing a gene?
column28: Transcription needs a DNA template, RNA polymerase and RNA nucleotides to build with. Ribosomes are only needed later, for translation.
column29: Which item reads mRNA rather than making it?

column9: Why is it important that translation begins at the start codon?
column14: It sets where reading begins, so the bases are grouped into the correct codons
column15: It is the only codon that does not code for an amino acid
column16: It turns the mRNA into tRNA
column17: It attaches the mRNA back to the DNA
column28: Starting at the right base means every following group of three is read correctly. The start codon does code for an amino acid (methionine); it is the stop codons that code for none.
column29: What would happen if the ribosome started one base too early?

column9: Select every event that happens outside the nucleus of a human cell. Select all that apply.
column14: A ribosome links amino acids together
column15: RNA polymerase copies a gene into mRNA
column16: A tRNA picks up a free amino acid
column17: The DNA of a gene unwinds so it can be copied
column18: A finished amino acid chain folds into shape
column19: RNA nucleotides pair with a DNA template
column28: Translation, tRNAs picking up amino acids and protein folding all happen in the cytoplasm. Everything involving the DNA template or RNA polymerase is transcription, which happens in the nucleus.
column29: Anything that touches DNA happens inside the nucleus.

column9: Match each mRNA codon to the tRNA anticodon that pairs with it.
column28: Pair every base: A–U and C–G. For example UCA pairs with AGU. A common slip is to reverse the order of the bases instead of pairing them one by one.
column29: Pair the first base of the codon with the first base of the anticodon, and so on.

column9: Cells that develop into red blood cells make huge amounts of hemoglobin, a protein. Which structure would you expect to find in large numbers in their cytoplasm?
column28: Hemoglobin is a protein, and proteins are built at ribosomes, so these cells are packed with them. Chloroplasts and cell walls are plant structures.
column29: Which structure builds proteins?

column9: A cell's nuclear pores are blocked so nothing can pass through them. What happens to protein synthesis?
column14: Proteins are built inside the nucleus instead
column15: Transcription cannot start, because RNA polymerase is outside the nucleus
column16: Nothing changes, because DNA leaves the nucleus another way
column17: mRNA is made but cannot reach the ribosomes, so new proteins are not built
column28: Transcription still happens in the nucleus, but the mRNA is trapped and the ribosomes in the cytoplasm never get it. Saying transcription stops confuses where the block is.
column29: Which molecule needs to leave the nucleus?

column9: True or false: A ribosome can begin translation at any codon on the mRNA.
column28: False. Translation begins at the start codon, AUG. Starting anywhere else would group the bases into the wrong codons.
column29: There is a special codon that marks the beginning.

column9: A classmate says transcription and translation are basically the same because both "copy" information. What is the key difference?
column14: Transcription happens at ribosomes; translation happens in the nucleus
column15: There is no difference; the words mean the same thing
column16: Transcription keeps the base "language" (DNA to RNA); translation changes it into amino acids (RNA to protein)
column17: Transcription builds proteins; translation builds DNA
column28: Transcription rewrites bases as bases, like copying notes by hand. Translation changes bases into a different kind of molecule, amino acids, like translating English into Spanish. The location choice is reversed.
column29: Think about what the words transcript and translate mean in an English class.

column9: An mRNA has 27 bases from the first base of the start codon through the last base of the stop codon. How many amino acids will be in the finished chain?
column28: 27 ÷ 3 = 9 codons. The stop codon adds no amino acid, so 9 − 1 = 8. Answering 9 counts the stop codon as an amino acid.
column29: Count the codons, then think about which codon doesn't add anything.

column9: A protein chain has 120 amino acids. How many mRNA bases are needed from the start codon through the stop codon?
column28: 120 amino acids need 120 codons, plus 1 stop codon = 121 codons. 121 × 3 = 363 bases. Answering 360 forgets the stop codon.
column29: Don't forget the codon that ends translation.

column9: An mRNA coding region is 300 bases long, counting the start codon and the stop codon. How many peptide bonds are in the finished amino acid chain?
column28: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 codons. The stop codon adds nothing, so there are 99 amino acids. A chain of 99 amino acids has 98 bonds between them. Answers of 100 or 99 skip one of these steps.
column29: A chain of 3 beads has only 2 links between them.

column9: A DNA template strand reads TAC AGA ATC. Codons: AUG = Met, UCU = Ser, AGA = Arg, AUC = Ile, UAG = stop. What amino acid chain is made?
column28: Transcribe first: TAC → AUG, AGA → UCU, ATC → UAG. That is Met, Ser, then stop. Choosing Arg – Ile comes from looking up the DNA triplets as if they were codons.
column29: Transcribe all three triplets before you touch the codon list.

column9: An mRNA strand reads CUA GGU. Which DNA template strand was it transcribed from?
column28: Pair each mRNA base with its DNA partner: C→G, U→A, A→T, G→C, G→C, U→A gives GAT CCA. GAU CCA wrongly puts U in DNA, and CTA GGT just swaps U for T without pairing.
column29: DNA uses T, never U. Pair each base rather than copying it.

column9: A DNA template triplet reads ATG. It is transcribed into an mRNA codon, and a tRNA pairs with that codon. The tRNA anticodon is ___.
column28: ATG → mRNA UAC → anticodon AUG. The anticodon matches the DNA template except that U replaces T. Typing ATG is the common error, since tRNA is RNA.
column29: Do it in two steps: DNA to mRNA, then mRNA to tRNA.

column9: Translate the mRNA AUG GUC AAU UGA GGA CCC. Codons: AUG = Met, GUC = Val, AAU = Asn, UGA = stop, GGA = Gly, CCC = Pro.
column14: Met – Val – Asn – Met – Gly – Pro
column28: The ribosome reads Met, Val, Asn and then hits UGA, a stop codon, and releases the chain. The codons after the stop are never translated, which is the trap in the longer answers.
column29: What does the ribosome do when it reaches a stop codon in the middle?

column9: An mRNA reads GCAUGUUUGGAUAA. Codons: AUG = Met, UUU = Phe, GGA = Gly, UAA = stop, GCA = Ala, UGU = Cys, UUG = Leu, GAU = Asp. What chain does the ribosome make?
column28: The ribosome starts at the first AUG (bases 3 to 5), then reads UUU, GGA and stops at UAA: Met – Phe – Gly. Reading from the very first base gives Ala – Cys – Leu – Asp, which ignores the start codon.
column29: Don't start at the first letter. Find AUG first.

column9: A student draws a model of protein synthesis in a human cell. Select every part of the model that is an ERROR. Select all that apply.
column14: The mRNA is drawn with thymine (T) bases
column15: tRNA anticodons are drawn pairing with mRNA codons
column16: Translation is drawn happening inside the nucleus
column17: The mRNA is drawn leaving through a nuclear pore
column18: The stop codon is drawn carrying an amino acid
column19: Amino acids are drawn joined in a chain at the ribosome
column28: mRNA has uracil, not thymine; translation happens at ribosomes in the cytoplasm, not in the nucleus; and stop codons carry no amino acid. The other three parts of the model are correct.
column29: Check each part against three rules: RNA bases, locations, and what a stop codon does.

column9: A student claims: "tRNA reads the DNA in the nucleus and carries amino acids there to build the protein." Which correction is best?
column14: tRNA pairs with mRNA codons at the ribosome in the cytoplasm; it never reads DNA
column15: tRNA reads DNA, but it builds proteins in the mitochondria
column16: The claim is correct as written
column17: mRNA, not tRNA, carries amino acids into the nucleus
column28: DNA is read by RNA polymerase during transcription. tRNA works during translation, matching its anticodon to mRNA codons at the ribosome. No protein is built in the nucleus.
column29: Which molecule does a tRNA anticodon actually pair with?

column9: Scientists add radioactive uracil to cells growing in a dish. A few minutes later, where will they first find the radioactivity?
column14: In newly made RNA in the nucleus
column15: In finished proteins in the cytoplasm
column16: In newly made DNA in the nucleus
column17: In the lipids of the cell membrane
column28: Uracil is used only in RNA, and RNA is made by transcription in the nucleus. Later the label would move to the cytoplasm with the mRNA. DNA does not use uracil, and proteins are made of amino acids, not bases.
column29: Which molecule uses uracil, and where is it made?

column9: A cell has plenty of mRNA and ribosomes, but all of its tRNA is destroyed. What happens?
column14: Proteins are built anyway, using mRNA bases as amino acids
column15: Ribosomes can't get amino acids matched to the codons, so no protein chains are built
column16: The mRNA turns into tRNA to replace it
column17: Transcription stops because tRNA makes mRNA
column28: tRNA is the adapter that brings each amino acid to its codon. Without it, translation stops even though the message is there. tRNA has nothing to do with making mRNA.
column29: What job does tRNA do at the ribosome?

column9: Put these events in order, from a gene in the nucleus to a finished chain.
column14: The ribosome reaches a stop codon and releases the chain
column15: A tRNA anticodon pairs with a codon inside the ribosome
column16: A ribosome finds the start codon on the mRNA
column17: The finished mRNA moves out through a nuclear pore
column18: RNA polymerase pairs RNA nucleotides with the DNA template
column19: A peptide bond joins the new amino acid to the growing chain
column28: Transcription comes first, then the mRNA leaves the nucleus, the ribosome finds the start codon, tRNAs pair with codons, peptide bonds form, and the stop codon ends it. A common error is placing the peptide bond before the tRNA arrives with the amino acid.
column29: An amino acid must arrive before it can be bonded to the chain.

column9: Tryptophan (Trp) has only one codon, UGG. Which DNA template triplet codes for tryptophan?
column28: Pair each mRNA base back to DNA: U→A, G→C, G→C gives ACC. TGG just swaps U for T (that is not the template), UGG contains U, and ACG would give the codon UGC.
column29: Work backward from the mRNA one base at a time, using DNA bases.

column9: An mRNA codon reads GUU. The DNA template triplet it was transcribed from is ___.
column28: G pairs with C, and each U on the mRNA pairs with an A on the DNA, giving CAA. Typing CTT is the common mistake: it changes U to T instead of finding the partner base.
column29: Find each base's partner. A U in mRNA came from a DNA A.

column9: Alanine has four codons: GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG. Select every DNA template triplet that would lead to alanine being added. Select all that apply.
column28: Transcribe each choice: CGA → GCU, CGG → GCC, CGT → GCA and CGC → GCG are all alanine. GCA → CGU and GCT → CGA are arginine codons; picking them comes from matching the DNA letters to the codon list without transcribing.
column29: Transcribe each triplet first, then compare to the four codons.

column9: Why doesn't a stop codon add an amino acid to the chain?
column14: No tRNA has an anticodon that matches a stop codon, so the chain is released instead
column15: Stop codons are found on tRNA, not mRNA
column16: The stop codon's amino acid is cut off right after it is added
column17: Stop codons are made of DNA, not RNA
column28: Stop codons have no matching tRNA, so nothing is delivered and the ribosome lets the chain go. Stop codons are on mRNA, like all codons.
column29: Amino acids arrive on tRNAs. What if no tRNA fits?

column9: Scientists add a drug that blocks transcription to cells and measure protein production. Proteins keep being made for about an hour, then production drops to nearly zero. What is the best explanation?
column14: Proteins are made from DNA directly, so they didn't need mRNA
column15: mRNA already made before the drug kept being translated until it broke down, and no new mRNA replaced it
column16: The drug blocks translation directly, but works slowly
column17: The cells ran out of DNA after an hour
column28: Blocking transcription stops new mRNA, but existing mRNA can still be translated for a while. Once it breaks down, protein production stops. The delay is the clue that translation itself was not blocked.
column29: Why would there be a delay instead of an instant stop?

column9: An mRNA reads AUG CAU CCG GAA UGG UAA. How many tRNAs deliver an amino acid while this mRNA is translated?
column28: There are 6 codons, but UAA is a stop codon with no tRNA. So 5 tRNAs deliver 5 amino acids. Answering 6 counts the stop codon.
column29: One tRNA per amino acid. How many codons actually code for an amino acid?

column9: In bacteria, ribosomes can start translating an mRNA while it is still being transcribed. Why can't this happen in human cells?
column15: In human cells transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm, so the mRNA must leave first
column28: The nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation in eukaryotes, so mRNA must be finished and exported before ribosomes reach it. Bacteria have no nucleus, so both steps share the cytoplasm.
column29: Think about the one big structure human cells have that bacteria lack.

column9: Which mRNA would be translated into exactly three amino acids and then stop?
column28: AUG UUC GGA UAG starts at AUG, adds three amino acids and ends at the stop codon UAG. AUG UUC UAG GGA stops after only two amino acids, AUG UUC GGA CUU never reaches a stop codon, and UUC GGA UAG AUG does not begin with the start codon.
column29: Look for a start codon first and a stop codon right after three amino acids.

column9: A bacterium's DNA template strand reads TACCGGATT. Type the nine-base mRNA transcribed from it, with no spaces: ___
column20: AUGGCCUAA|AUG GCC UAA|A U G G C C U A A|AUG-GCC-UAA|A-U-G-G-C-C-U-A-A
column28: T→A, A→U, C→G, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U, T→A, T→A gives AUGGCCUAA (AUG GCC UAA). Writing any T or swapping A↔T instead of A→U is the usual error.
column29: Split it into triplets first: TAC CGG ATT.

column9: Codons: UUU = Phe, AAA = Lys. A tRNA with the anticodon AAA arrives at the ribosome. Which amino acid is it carrying?
column17: No amino acid; AAA is a stop signal
column28: The anticodon AAA pairs with the mRNA codon UUU, and the chart says UUU = Phe. Choosing Lys comes from looking up the anticodon on the chart instead of the codon.
column29: Codon charts list mRNA codons. Find the codon this anticodon pairs with.

column9: A finished protein chain has exactly 10 amino acids. Select every statement that must be true. Select all that apply.
column14: Its mRNA has 33 bases from the start of the start codon through the end of the stop codon
column16: tRNAs made 10 deliveries of amino acids to build it
column18: Its mRNA has exactly 10 codons including the stop codon
column19: It was built inside the nucleus
column28: 10 amino acids need 10 codons plus a stop codon: 11 × 3 = 33 bases. One tRNA delivers each amino acid (10), and 10 amino acids have 9 bonds between them. Forgetting the stop codon or counting bonds as equal to amino acids are the traps.
column29: Count carefully: amino acids, codons, links between amino acids.

column9: Which statement best explains why the order of bases in a gene matters?
column14: It sets which sugar the protein is made of
column15: It sets the order of codons, which sets the order of amino acids, which decides how the protein folds and works
column16: It only matters for DNA replication, not for proteins
column17: It decides how many ribosomes the cell has
column28: Base order → codon order → amino acid order → folded shape → job. Proteins are built from amino acids, not sugars, and a gene's bases matter for proteins, not just for copying DNA.
column29: Follow the chain of cause and effect from DNA to the folded protein.
